title: Honi and the carob tree
hook: an old man plants a tree that won't fruit for seventy years, for his grandchildren (Talmud, Taanit 23a)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel taught the whole Torah on one foot, and ended: now go and learn. What did you learn? Day fifty-eight.

Think of something you enjoy today that somebody started long before you were born. The park you walk through, planted by a city a hundred years ago. A library. A recipe your great-grandmother worked out. A tree whose shade you sit in. Someone made it, knowing they would never see you. The Talmud has a story about this, and about a man named Honi. He was a famous holy man in the land of Israel, around the first century BCE, known as Honi the Circle-Drawer, because once, in a drought, he drew a circle on the ground and would not step out of it until it rained. One day Honi is walking along a road, and he sees an old man planting a tree. Today's story is Honi and the carob tree.
screen: `SOMEONE STARTED IT FOR YOU.` → `HONI THE CIRCLE-DRAWER.` → `AN OLD MAN PLANTING A TREE.`

segments.voice: The story begins with a verse that bothered Honi. A psalm about the return from exile, which in the King James words reads: "When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream." Seventy years in exile, like a dream. Can a person really sleep seventy years? So Honi is on the road, turning that over, and he sees the old man planting a carob tree. Honi asks: how long until this tree gives fruit? Seventy years, says the man. And Honi asks: are you so sure you'll live another seventy years? And the old man says, more or less: I found carob trees in the world when I came into it. My ancestors planted them for me. So I'm planting these for my children. Then Honi sits down to eat, and falls asleep. Rocks grow up around him, hiding him, and he sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that same tree. Are you the one who planted it? Honi asks. No, says the man. I'm his grandson. The Talmud's story goes on, and it ends sadly: back home, nobody believes he's Honi, and he feels so alone that he no longer wants to live. The rabbis draw from it a saying, companionship or death. But the heart of the first part is the old man, planting. He does the work, and the fruit belongs to someone he'll never meet. That's how every one of us got here: under trees we didn't plant.
screen: `WE WERE LIKE THEM THAT DREAM.` · `ARE YOU SURE YOU'LL LIVE SEVENTY YEARS?` · `MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME.` · `I'M HIS GRANDSON.` · then, large: `FOR THE ONES AFTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant or start something for someone later. For now, settle, and breathe, and look around. Find one thing near you that someone made or planted before you: a tree outside, a building, a word you use. Thank them silently, whoever they were. Then think of one small thing you could start today for someone after you. A seed in a pot. A note for your kids. Money set aside. A skill you teach. Pick one. The bell holds the time.
Honi and the carob tree. An old man plants a tree that won't fruit for seventy years, because his ancestors planted for him. Today's word.
screen: `HONI AND THE CAROB TREE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for the ones after. Today, do one small thing whose fruit you may never see. Plant it anyway. Day fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews tell the story of Honi and the carob tree especially on Tu BiShvat, the new year of the trees, when many plant trees in Israel and elsewhere; the story itself is in the Talmud, Taanit 23a.

original.note: Hebrew, haruv: the carob tree, slow to bear fruit.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who sleeps for seventy years.
what it means: we all live under trees we didn't plant, so we plant for the ones after.
what a scholar hears: Taanit 23a, a story built around Psalm 126:1, told of Honi ha-Me'agel, the circle-drawer, with a sadder ending than most retellings keep.

notes: Taanit 23a paraphrased; the sad ending and Rava's saying ('either companionship or death') included briefly. Confirm the attribution and tone.
Honi dated to 'around the first century BCE'; confirm.
Psalm 126:1 quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 may be preferred by a Jewish Keeper (and numbers it the same).
Carob taking seventy years to fruit is the story's figure, not botany; the script frames it as the man's answer.
